Interviewer:	Right, the project I’m doing is looking at women engineering students, well mainly engineering students that are going on placement this summer, but we are interviewing some people that have decided not to go on placement as well. And we’re basically exploring women’s first experiences in the industry – what they expect and their career expectations and that sort of thing. Then we will compare it to their experiences when they’re actually in the industry and what we’re really trying to do is improve the retention of women in the industry. So we’re looking to see if work meets women’s expectations and things like that. So I’ve got a few questions to ask you and I’ll just start off asking you some background questions about why you decided to do engineering. Is it civil engineering you’re doing?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	What A levels did you do?

Subject:	Maths, physics and French.

Interviewer:	OK, French? What type of school did you go to?

Subject:	Just a normal boring –comprehensive. 

Interviewer:	Not a girls’ school or anything like that?

Subject:	Oh, no.

Interviewer:	Have you got any previous work experience?

Subject:	Yeah, I went on site last summer.

Interviewer:	OK, are you a sponsored student?

Subject:	No, I just wrote off saying please can I have a job, to a few companies – and one of them said yeah, we could do with some – well, slave labour basically – so come along.

Interviewer:	What do your parents do? Are either of them engineers at all?

Subject:	No, they’re accountants.

Interviewer:	OK so when and why do you think you decided to do engineering?

Subject:	Er, I didn’t really think about it till I was looking through like prospectuses. It just never really occurred to me, because my school was a bit non-practical and then like career wise they never sort of really mentioned engineering and things like that. They sort of – law and history and things like that and that’s the sort of thing they try and push you into. And so I don’t think it was until after I read the prospectus and then I was reading through and my mum said well, you could do this – I didn’t like anything I was like, I don’t want to do this, it’s sort of worky, too much sitting around reading. My mum was like try engineering, you haven’t read it. I thought, oh that sounds fun, it’s quite me. Sort of you know, practical work basically – so I’m not sitting around, in an office. I get bored and that’s where I came from, really no major reason.

Interviewer:	So you didn’t really have any careers advice that pointed you in that direction?

Subject:	I didn’t have a single careers interview through school no, they don’t really mention – like I say they seem to be very, well old school as it were. Oxford, Cambridge – trying to send as many people as they could off to do law and history and English and things.

Interviewer:	OK, you said that your mum helped you decide on engineering – has your family been quite supportive then of the fact that you…?

Subject:	Yeah, I mean basically it was I thought about it, thought it was a good idea. I mean my parents weren’t particularly fussed. I mean there were more pleased that I was doing this because it’s vocational. I mean if I’d just sort of gone, I’m going to do English, my mum would have been like, ‘what? What are you going to do afterwards?’ Yeah, so they’re supportive in that, but they’re not really bothered what I do. In fact, it’s more like I choose what I want to do and they’re happy that I’m happy.

Interviewer:	OK, did you do much career research apart from looking at the university prospectuses? Why engineering more than any other choice?

Subject:	Once I’d thought about it, I sort of looked it up a bit on the Internet, but not massively.

Interviewer:	OK, how did you decide to do civil engineering and not say mechanical or electrical?

Subject:	That came to me from reading through loads and loads of different university prospectuses and seeing which course I liked the sound of the most. And I liked the sound of civils the most.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think it is that does appeal to you about the course?

Subject:	I think, like I say I think it’s the practical nature of it, because I’m really not just the kind of sit around permanently, type of person. I think that the idea – and actually physically creating something – where we can design it all but then you can actually physically see your work happen, whereas with a lot of other subjects, you know, it’s all up there, it’s all these ideas and theories and you don’t see it happen and I think if you design a building, you know, 4 years later or something, it’s there and you’ll be like, I did that. And I think, I like that.

Interviewer:	Ok, did you know that you wanted to do the placement course from the beginning?

Subject:	Yes, because I thought – basically everybody I spoke to, like when we came on visits and spoke to students and stuff, they all said that it was a really good idea. Plus I liked the idea of having a break in the middle – it’s just a break from the studying because I thought it would be nice to have weekends – (lost words) – you just don’t have weekends when you’re at university. You can’t just go, yeah, great no work.

Interviewer:	How did you decide to come to [this university] then?

Subject:	Erm, that was I read a load of prospectuses, it was really good for civil engineering and I came up here for a visit and just thought, wow, because I wanted to be on – I wanted a campus university and I came up and thought, wow, this is really nice – and that was that.

Interviewer:	OK, when you decided to do engineering did you realise that it was so male dominated? 

Subject:	I knew it was, but there’s actually less – there’s actually more girls than I thought there was going to be.

Interviewer:	Really?

Subject:	Yes, on our bit of the course. There seems to be more on our actual course than there are in other years.

Interviewer:	What sort of proportions are there?

Subject:	I think there’s 10 girls, on the civil.

Interviewer:	Out of how many?

Subject:	80? There’s not many but there’s more than I thought there was going to be.

Interviewer:	Does that bother you, that …?

Subject:	Not really, because I mean we’re just treated as people. I mean, yes, we are the girls sometimes but they don’t – I mean other boys on our – on our course, don’t treat us girls – girls in that respect – I mean obviously girls, you know you’re a girl you can’t do anything. So, I mean, we might just be lucky, I don’t know but…

Interviewer:	Do you think that more women should be encouraged to take engineering?

Subject:	I – I mean I don’t know, I just thought – I mean, for me, I just think from my school, I think anybody should have been encouraged to do engineering because it just didn’t seem to be mentioned. I mean, in general, I just think the whole – and especially for girls, because I think a lot of girls are still like, oh it’s a boy thing, because you still get it now. You tell people that you’re here and they expect you to say Sociology or something and you go and say engineering and they’re like, really? So I just think – yeah, I think there should be, like at schools, just to make sure people realise that – because I think a lot of girls, are like oh I’m going to look all boyish and OK, and I was like – because a lot of times you see a talk, at the risk of being rude – a lot of the time you see these big, kind of manly women, then you just get that image in mind, and I think you need to make sure they know that there’s like normal, girly girls because we all have our make-up bags.

Interviewer:	Do you think there needs to be more information about what engineering really is? 

Subject:	I think so, because you say civil engineering and everyone assumes I’m going to be working – they presume I’m working on a building site. So, yes, I do – do work on a building site but I don’t, you know, wander around with a hod carrier or something and I think yeah, because a part of that is image and as soon as you say civil, people think building sites, people think you are a builder. They don’t understand that you can be like the engineer – you’re supervising or something, so I think there probably should be more information about what actually goes on, on site, because this is very much a man building physically image.

Interviewer:	OK. What characteristics do you think make a good engineer?

Subject:	I – I don’t know. I think you have to be very able to deal with a crisis, because I didn’t work as an engineer on site, I just got a job in a lab but I did see the engineers around and from what other people have said to me I think you need to be able to cope in a crisis because it sounds like they have a lot. I think you need to be able to be a boss without being sort of you know like have the authority without being bossy as it were, without – being able to tell people what to do without ordering them around.

Interviewer:	Yeah, so being a good manager.

Subject:	Yeah, I think – I think that’s a big help and just generally being – having a laugh about it. Like if things go wrong, there’s no point in having massive stress because it’s just gonna make it worse.

Interviewer:	Do you think that any of those characteristics are more male or more female?

Subject:	Er, I think it’s – I couldn’t say whether it’s male or female, I think it depends on the person – more on the person as to how they’d react to things rather than being able to say a male would do this, a female would do that. I think it’s a personal…

Interviewer:	OK, so do you think there any advantages to being a woman engineer?

Subject:	Well, when I was on site, I mean I did have a lot – like that I was sort of like the pet, as it were. I mean there might have been – I was working at terminal 5 so there was a lot of people there, but work inside the company must have been a good – there was a lot of people and they all knew who I was. So, in a way it’s good, because they all know who you are and they all know who you work, and generally speaking I found that it worked to my advantage, like you’d go off for some help for something and you’d get it. I mean I know part of that was the whole of being 19, on a building site and there was a lot of old men around, sort of playing on that one a bit, but I think – I really (?) because a lot – certainly around the people, especially the men, are very determined to show they’re not sexist. So, in some ways it can go the other way and sometimes they’re a bit too liberal and you’re just like oh I can’t do it because I’m – you know like, carrying things like there’s equality and there’s a stupidness, because I had that a few times like, oh if we can carry that and I was saying no. Equal to a point and then…

Interviewer:	In your experience so far, do you think that there are any disadvantages then? Like what you just said?

Subject:	As a bit, I mean that was more probably when I was trying to be big and strong, trying to carry really heavy stuff but generally I found it to be – everyone who worked here was really fine. They’d be like, oh no, you go and lift something really heavy and they’d go oh no, let me do that for you and generally I thought it worked quite well. I mean there were a few people and they’d be a bit like, you’re a girl, what are you doing here? But it’s to be expected, you’re gonna get that from people that are gonna think that.

Interviewer:	Yeah, were there other women working on the site?

Subject:	They kept maintaining there were. (laughter) It took me about a month before I saw one. They insisted there were other women on site. I think I saw 2 going on site, but then again it was a huge site so there could well have been. There wasn’t many - they were rare, I should say. It was quite surprising if you saw one, if you ever saw another female sort of engineer around but…

Interviewer:	OK, we’ll probably come back to that, after placement and that, a bit later on but I’m going to ask you a few questions about the course itself? Has the course been what you expected it to be?

Subject:	I don’t really know because I didn’t really come with any expectations as it were. I mean it may sound a bit silly but because I didn’t really know what I was letting myself in for. It seems a little – it’s less practical than I thought it was going to be. I don’t know really how I thought it was going to be more practical but there’s definitely a lot more learning and sort of less actual hands-on than I thought there was going to be but I’m not really – I didn’t really know what to expect when I came so …

Interviewer:	Yeah, now that you’re here, do you think that this course should be more practical?

Subject:	Er, it’s not so much about the actual practical stuff, it’s practical applications, you know do certain things and it’s like you sit there and they do it different to like if you go out in the industry, it’s done a different way and you do sort of sit there looking at your lecturers, going you’re telling us all this, but when was the last time you actually went out and you did – on site – something like the surveying equipment. They know how to use it, but we’ve been taught methods and a couple of my friends went out and told them what they’d learnt on site and they were like, that’s ridiculous we don’t do this – we use this way. And while it’s good knowing all the theory you do sometimes – I do sometimes wonder when the last time they applied it in the industry was and they generally speaking, they seem to keep up quite well, so it’s just like the odd 1 or 2 lecturers, you know, sort of think well, you don’t really know.

Interviewer:	So do you think it would actually help more, in terms of when you’re actually going into the industry, if things were a little bit more up to date?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Maybe when they’re talking about theory they say this is how you would use it?

Subject:	Or maybe, if we got taken to site occasionally, because I mean I happened to get a job on site – that’s the first time I’d ever been on a site, and I just happened to get a job there. And there’s people on the course that’s still – you know, they’ve nearly done 2 years now and they still haven’t actually set foot on a building site.

Interviewer:	Yes, there haven’t been any site visits or anything?

Subject:	No, I mean they do – they do have a – this is like sort of CIVSOC which does site visits but a lot of people aren’t a member, and it’s not organised by the department, and you end up missing lectures and things so – it’s not, I just think maybe they should organise the occasional one as part of the course somewhere, like ‘cos then if everybody’s going on a day then…

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think have been the best and the worse things about the course so far? 

Subject:	Erm, the best I think – I mean I do think there’s a quite a good mix of stuff we learn and as I said the people – I think we’re quite a novel course in that we all get on, as in we’re all actually friends. Whereas a lot of people, it’s not that they don’t get on, they’re just not particularly friendly. Whereas everybody’s really friendly with each other, so you feel you could do any sort of group work and you know you’re gonna have a friend as it were, in your group, you’re not gonna get stuck with people you’re just like, oh my God, who are you? So that’s nice. Erm, the worst bit is there’s just some of the - some of the work we do, you just sit and you’re just like why? Why do I need to know this? Or why are we learning it now? I think we could have spent more time on other stuff that, you know, why have we sort of learnt this? Like some of the water stuff’s been – literally, excuse the pun, but gone straight in at the deep-end and we’re just like why are we learning it, its too technical, why are we learning it now? So, that’s definitely been one of the worse things.

Interviewer:	Do you get any opportunities to feed those sorts of comments back?

Subject:	Yeah, there will be a module, a review performance, when we have staff/student meetings, we can pass on our comments via the course rep and they can say them at the meeting and pass them on to lecturers.

Interviewer:	OK, have you been taught by any female lecturers?

Subject:	We have, we’ve got one female lecturer.

Interviewer:	Do you think they treat you the same as the male lecturers?

Subject:	Erm, if anything I’d have said, in work related, like handing in, she’s harder – as in she’s more strict. She’s like, this is the rule and that’s it. Again, that might just be personal.

Interviewer:	Yeah it’s a bit difficult when you’ve only got one female, to make a generalisation.

Subject:	Yeah, but generally, yeah, it’s all the same. I haven’t noticed any difference.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the male lecturers treat the female and male students the same?

Subject:	Yeah. I’ve not noticed any difference.

Interviewer:	Do you think that you’d find it encouraging to have more female lecturers?

Subject:	Erm, possibly. I mean to be – it never sort of struck me, I know, that’s a bad thing to say, not vocalizing a lot of things. I don’t think it makes much difference, I mean as long as they know the subject then I really don’t think that male/female makes all that much difference. I mean it might help a bit if we had more females that had been out on site and they related it to talking, on site, perhaps. That may help but I wouldn’t necessarily say that it made that much difference. As long as they know their subject, I don’t think it matters.

Interviewer:	Have you got a personal tutor?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Are they male or female?

Subject:	Male.

Interviewer:	And are you happy about that or would you rather have a female?

Subject:	Erm, I’m happy that they’re male because if I have any real confidential female issues, I’d go to a lecturer or something – I would go to one of my female – if I needed to – yeah, I mean if I had any major issues that I needed to – I’d go to someone else, but…

Interviewer:	OK, do you think your tutor has got – are they approachable?

Subject:	Yeah, he’s very nice.

Interviewer:	OK, who or what do you think has been the biggest influence on you since you started this degree?

Subject:	Erm, I really don’t know. That’s quite a hard thing to answer. Probably more the friends on my course, to be honest, because they’re there all the time, I talk to them all the time about like the year out – how and like you know, they had the big debate of should we do or should we not, you know some of us are and some of us aren’t, and then it’s a why aren’t you? It’s been a why aren’t you/why are you situation and it all sort of talks like that. I think it’s probably actually the – more like work and stuff, like all the little things like module choices, you know, when you’re stuck – and you’re just like, what are you doing? You end up doing what all your friends are doing, so you can work together.

Interviewer:	OK, do you have to do much group work?

Subject:	Yeah, we normally have a sort of a big group project, we haven’t actually got one this semester but we’ve had some smaller – most of the subjects we have some form of, normally sort of groups of 4 or something for just little bits of work.

Interviewer:	When you have to work in groups how do you decide who to work with?

Subject:	Sometimes you get put in, like alphabetically or whatever, they just stick us in groups and other times we’re just – at lot of the time its who you’re sat with - because we’re friends, some of the assignments it’s who you’re sort of sat with, as it were. You’re sort of like, yeah, 1,2,3,4, - 1,2,3,4, type thing. Or just sort of my closer friends, I think, I tend to work with because we get on quite well.

Interviewer:	Yeah, OK. Do you prefer to work with women or men or doesn’t it matter?

Subject:	Er, it doesn’t matter because I think – because we’re all quite similar, like they’re only a few girls and we’re all sort of quite similar personalities, it doesn’t really make that much difference because, like I said, the girls on our course, we all tend to get in a big tizz about things but then so do the boys, they get just as stressed and just as wound up, so – so it doesn’t really make a difference.

Interviewer:	Have you had any particularly good or bad experiences of group work?

Subject:	Erm, I have had some bad ones but then again that’s probably slightly more down to individual personalities.

Interviewer:	Yeah, what sorts of things happened?

Subject:	Well there’s a been a couple of people and when you get split in alphabetical – there’s a couple of people and they’re both 

Interviewer:	The same people?

Subject:	Well, there’s me an my friend and we fight like cats and dogs on work but its all friendly, as in we’ll bicker and we’ll go on at each other non-stop, but, at the end of the day, we just agree to disagree or something and you know, we’ll walk out the meeting and we’re still best of friends kind of thing and it makes others laugh and we’ll be at each other’s throats but then, at the end of the day, we just went, OK you’re right, I surrender but there’s a couple of people and they’re like really quiet and in a group situation, it drives you mad because I end up being really bossy (yeah) because it’s like if you’ve got work to give out and everyone’s like, I don’t mind, I don’t mind, I don’t mind, I get really frustrated and start dishing out the work because they don’t want to, they’re just sat there going oh it doesn’t bother me. I’m like that to a point, you know, I don’t particularly have a preference, but then if no one’s got a preference I’ll be like, well then, I do have a preference if nobody else does and there’s a couple of people they just don’t speak at all. So you can have a group meeting and they’ll sort of be sat in a corner and like I know they’re thinking, you know, we’ll be putting ideas sort of down on a table and you know they’re there. One of them, if you specifically ask, will then say it to you and that does irritate me, because I know they’re thinking it and you’re like, just say it. It doesn’t matter if it’s stupid, I mean you’re laughing half of my ideas down. You’ve just got to keep – especially, on things like design projects, like ideas for a building, you’ve just to keep producing pictures and it’s again, generally speaking, the people who are very quiet drive you nuts.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the group work will help you when you get in the industry?

Subject:	I think it will because, like I’ve said, you learn how to deal, you learn that to sit and shouting with each other doesn’t always work. Sometimes it helps and I get my way but – no, you sort of learn, because you learn important things now, like you learn that sitting, shouting at each other around the table, you learn that you can’t argue you have to learn – you learn when to compromise, I find that you learn sort of when you can and can’t – like you can learn what you can compromise on, on a design or something you can just go OK, then, we’re never going to decide so let’s do this one. I think it’ll help because you’ve got all the – a little bit of fighting out of you for when you’re going and it starts to really matter, in a job.

Interviewer:	OK, are there any other particular things on your course, teaching or advice that you’ve had that you think will help you on your placement and when you go to work?

Subject:	Erm, we’ve had bits of things. Bits of things from one of my tutors about being – female – you know basically, you know the phrases, don’t put up with any crap. And he goes like, if you have – if someone gives you – if you – he was mainly talking to us girls at the time. I think we were just having a chat after one of the companies had been – if they like give you issues then he was like, then you do something about it. He was like don’t – ‘cos he was telling us this story about like 2 girls he knew and having to deal with some bully manager and one of them told him, ever so politely, where to go, and problem solved and you know, the other one ended up crying every day in the toilets kind of thing and things like saying like make sure you don’t have to deal with that. And probably…

Interviewer:	OK, what skills do you think you’ll take from the course into your placement?

Subject:	I think having a basic knowledge of different, different sort of applications like the surveying and other things like that, that you start to use. I think I have that and I think there’s a bit of general knowledge about site and I think we could have done more and we keep campaigning for like health and safety modules and things. But, I think there’s general awareness, mainly of how to work in a group, and I think the things that will be very different to anything that we’re expecting – but I think the sort of little things like how to work in a group and how to get along in a situation where you don’t like it, because you sort of learn to put up and do your work here, so I think that will help.

Interviewer:	Do you think that anything from your summer placement will help you on your work placement?

Subject:	Erm, hopefully because I had an awful – I did meet a few sexist people in many issues over cups of tea, many, many issues over a cups of tea and me making it was a general issue and me refusing to make it because I didn’t have to. So little things like that will help. Putting up with a bit of general abuse from people because you know – like it was a friendly abuse but some of the time you’re just like really go away – I’m not in the mood today. So I think that’ll help and just generally having been a bit aware of what goes on, on site, and having been told off a few times by Foremen, now I realise you know – the first time it happens then when I do it for real on site, I’m not going to end up wanting to burst into tears, ‘cos the first time I got really shouted at I was a bit like, oh, but then I was like, I didn’t do anything wrong it was your mistake.

Interviewer:	How did you deal with like the sexism then, did they listen to you when you told them that you weren’t going to make cups of tea?

Subject:	Erm, eventually, it was done on a slightly immature level, but the message got through – ‘cos of where I was working, some of the people were – it sounds rude to say but less intelligent, they were. So, erm and like I said there were a couple of older guys and you could sort of see that they’d been in the industry since they were 16 – they were 40 odd so they’d been there a long time. It’s a bit like you know, new girls coming in – they’re still on the secretary image (yeah) – so eventually it got through after I complained and whinged and moaned at my supervisor. And then, he sort of noted it as it were, and paid attention to when they were asking me, and because there were sort of two sections in the lab, and they were even in a different one. And after I’d like whinged at all the people in my bit for a while, then they sort of started apologising then for telling me to – because they thought it was about tea, and 2 cups of tea is nothing compared to about 15 for them and that was alright. I mean, generally on site, it was – it was mostly compliments I got so I wasn’t – and I’m not particularly fazed by – you know, if someone comes and shouts something at you, you know, like talking about your bum or something – I’m oh thank you, that’s quite nice of you – that’s my general attitude. If I can’t – erm, I didn’t have any real issues with anyone.

Interviewer:	OK, do you feel quite prepared and ready to go on a placement now?

Subject:	I hope so. I think I am. I’m scared but that’s to do with working and a job, going to a new place with new people but generally speaking, yeah, I think I’m – I suppose I’m ready because I can cope.

Interviewer:	Do you think you were ready to go on site when you actually went on your summer job?

Subject:	I think I was, yeah. I mean there’s certain things you’re just never gonna appreciate till you get there and like I said, having 3000 people know your name and where you work is something. It’s a – until you walk past, around them and they’re like Hi, Hannah, how’re you doing? And you’re like, you know like, alright, who are you? How do you know my name? Things like that. I mean obviously I don’t – and that’s sort of prepared me to be known, as it were, so I’m expecting – maybe not quite on that scale – I think partly because of the nature of the work I did, because you’re in the lab, I mean I used to go out a lot, onto different bits of the site, and so – and you know I used to be like hey, and a lot of the time I was floating and so I was looking what different people did, so I went all over the place and a lot of people got to know me that way, but yes, I’m prepared to have a bit sort of strangers knowing my name, over the year.

Interviewer:	Do you think that’s a good thing or a bad thing that people know who you are?

Subject:	I can never decide. I mean it doesn’t really bother. I mean it’s nice in a way, because you could walk up to someone and they knew where I was or where I’d come from that so they didn’t have to sort of guess at what I was doing. So that was alright, but it didn’t strike me as a particularly bad thing. It was embarrassing at times.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the university could do anything else to help prepare you? More than what they have?

Subject:	Erm, only maybe a little bit of health and safety and probably cover sites a bit, and things like that. But I think part of the problem is that you’ve just got to go there and experience it, so I don’t really think they could have done much more – maybe just have a few lectures on health & safety.

Interviewer:	Did you say you’ve had like people from the industry, coming in and talking to you?

Subject:	Yeah, people from companies come for like – they come in the evening and do presentations (right) so it’s for the year’s out so it’s optional whether you attend.

Interviewer:	Have they been quite useful?

Subject:	Erm, it varies, depending on the company, but if you’re going to be mainly focussing on the year out, it’s telling you more about the company it’s not particularly site specific. But some of them have been really quite useful about the year out and a bit like – they’ve given a bit of examples about what you can expect to be doing – what work you can expect to do.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that they way you are taught and the whole sort of educational experience reflects what it is like in the industry?

Subject:	In a way, no but then again you’ve got to learn because it’s obviously a very classroom atmosphere but you have to learn and you can’t learn everything – you can’t learn all the theory out on site. Like I said maybe, just some of the lectures are just a bit out of date, so it’s just making sure they’re completely up to date on the some of things that they teach us but I do think – while it’s very different I don’t think it can be done any other way.

Interviewer:	OK, how did you decide to go on placement then? What things you do think will be good about it?

Subject:	I think actually having a break in between the years, yes, because I really need the time off and I’ll have chance in the middle as well, to work out if I really want to do civil engineering, because a lot of people are like I don’t want to do it anymore. Well, you don’t know unless you go on site. So, I don’t know, then if you have a cut – a break off, well it’s a year, but then I can finish my degree and look for another job straight away, rather than a – getting a job and getting out if I didn’t like it anymore. Having time in the middle to learn new things, apply things – and you’ll learn more stuff, and when you come – so when you come back you’ll be able to apply it. It’s like me saying things like, ‘cos I was in the lab, doing soils testing, and then this year we started on – we’ve not done any and then we started on soil module and there’s things like they mention as a throw away, like this test and I’d be like oh yeah, I remember that test and I could picture it, what I was doing and then he explained the theory, because I could imagine myself having been doing that, it helped a bit with the theory. So, I think, from personal experience that really helped, so I imagine after doing a year out, you’ll have a lot more experience of things like that and learn a lot more.

Interviewer:	OK, did anyone particularly encourage you or discourage you from going on placement?

Subject:	Erm, we do have quite a lot of talks and a couple of the lecturers do – they do encourage you to go but if you don’t want to do it, it’s not particularly a huge deal. They just see that we get informed of all the …

Interviewer:	Do you know any people that aren’t going on a placement?

Subject:	There’s not many off the course that aren’t, I don’t think.

Interviewer:	And why do you think that they decided not to?

Subject:	Erm, there’s a couple that are older. Erm, there’s a couple that are older and they’ve already done their HND’s and had experience in industry and they’ve been sent by their companies to get a degree (right, OK, yeah). So there’s a couple of them – they’re getting their degrees just to get (yeah) and so they just wanna go straight through and go back out to work. Erm, a couple of us again – there’s a couple that are older and want to get through. Similarly, there’s a couple of people that don’t really have a reason, ‘cos they have been asking them for their reason and they just say, ‘don’t have one’. But, no the majority of people, even I people I know that say they don’t want to do civil engineering as a career are still doing the year out, just because it’s the thing to do sort of thing.

Interviewer:	Yes. Would you say that one of the reasons you’re thinking of doing it, is to help make your mind up about whether you think it…

Subject:	Yeah, not least because if I do then want to do civil engineering, I’ll be able to choose within the field of civil engineering. Like when we come back and start choosing modules I’ll be able to be a bit more informed about what I’m choosing and not just go for the easiest modules. I might actually do something I like.

Interviewer:	Do you know where you’re going on your placement?

Subject:	Not yet, no, I just had my – just accepted an offer and they said they’ll be able to tell us nearer the time. I just know it’s in the south of England.

Interviewer:	So you know the company that you’re going with?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	OK, what attracted you to the company that you’re going with?

Subject:	Well, they came and did a presentation here and the guy that did the presentation was really nice and the company sounded – and the company’s quite a big company. Erm, I had an interview with them. Er, obviously they made me an offer. I had an offer from another company as well and the other company was really disorganised and it took them ages to get their letters out, and we only got our offer letters because we said, look we’ve got to apply to another company (right) in a few days – we’ve got to have sent off, so can we please have our offer letters. Again, we got them then – so it was a bit disorganised and when I got – it’s just the letter was very well written – the offer was nice but the letter was really well written; the information was already geared to me. And basically the main reason for choice between them, was because I couldn’t choose between the 2 companies, it basically came down to the letter they wrote. I thought it was nicer.

Interviewer:	OK, when you were sort of looking at those 2 companies, did you look at things like training opportunities and…?

Subject:	I did a bit, yeah. I mean I asked most of those questions in the interview. They both take – as a general rule they take on like sandwich students – companies tend to sort of train you and stuff. It seems to be the generally accepted thing to do.

Interviewer:	OK, did you do much research into the companies?

Subject:	I did a little bit. I looked at the web sites a bit, but I didn’t really find all that much.

Interviewer:	Did they both come and do presentations?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Have the university been very involved in helping find the placement for you?

Subject:	Erm, yeah, because we get told, like [placement co-ordinator] arranges with the company when the interviews are going to be, then he emails us and tells us when, like there’s going to be a presentation – and certain companies just send them through a job offer, saying can you – do you know anyone that’s interested? Like he sends those through to us. Basically everything he gets he sends through to us and says you know, come along if you’re interested you know, send an email to us if you’re interested. So he is quite, quite encouraging.

Interviewer:	Do you think there is anything else that he could do to help you?

Subject:	Well not – not really because I mean he – as soon as he gets the information on companies or presentations, he tells us and I don’t think there’s much more that can be done really.

Interviewer:	OK did you ever considered being sponsored?

Subject:	Yeah, I did.

Interviewer:	How did you decide not to do that?

Subject:	Well, basically it’s the MEng they go basically the entire of the MEng is really going to apply for sponsorship. Well it was quite easily decided for me, in that I didn’t get any interviews. (Oh right) In the long run, I’m glad I wasn’t (yes) because like I said I actually got – I then got 2 good companies, possibly better companies than some of the one’s that do sponsorship for – I’d rather work for (yes). Erm, and I got to choose between them and I had to choose. I know a few of my friends now, they got all sponsored – they were all pleased at the time because they get all their sponsorship money and stuff, but then a few of them have been like, oh I wish I could choose – like a couple of company’s having – seems to be having money troubles, and they’re stuck basically. So, er afterwards, after a year out, I might get sponsored by the company and that would be fine, that way round.

Interviewer:	Yeah, when you know whether you like the company or not?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	OK what do you think will be the best and the worst things about going on placement?

Subject:	Best thing I would say is to get experienced a bit and just a break and chance to do something different. Worst thing will probably be the weather in winter and if it’s anything like the summer I worked – the hours, they’re a bit long. Erm, and little things, like silly things I’m worried about, like getting out of the habit of working so when I come back from my year out, suddenly I think Oh God, I have to work again – it will be a nightmare.

Interviewer:	You’re looking at site work on your placement, or don’t you know yet?

Subject:	Er, I think it’ll be site work, well they aim to do that in your year.

Interviewer:	How do you expect work to differ from being at University?

Subject:	Er, little things like you’ll be able to like come home at night and the work stays at work. It’ll be like a Friday and I’ll be – the weekend, I’ll be really, yeah, it’s the weekend and they still have lots of work to do. So it’ll actually be the weekend and you’ll have no work to do and things like that. I don’t think – it’s going to be a whole different atmosphere, actually being able to leave your work behind and go home and not have anything else to do. It should be quite – it’ll be different, I haven’t had that for a while.

Interviewer:	In terms of your career, where do you see yourself in say 5 years time?

Subject:	I haven’t got a clue.

Interviewer:	Do you think that you will be in engineering?

Subject:	I think I probably will be, because I like it and I like all the ideas of it, so I probably still will be in civil engineering.

Interviewer:	And do you think that you’d like to go into managing people or do you want to stay on the technical side of things?

Subject:	I – well I don’t know. Part of that, hopefully, I’ll figure out, on my year out, just by being around people, seeing what they do.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think would be your ideal career?

Subject:	Oh, where I earn lots of money, in the warm (laughter). I think I really don’t know.

Interviewer:	Have you thought about doing the consultancy side of it instead of contracting?

Subject:	Yeah, that side didn’t particularly appeal to me. I’d rather be on the contracting, even if it does mean I have to go outside – I’d rather do contracting than consultancy because you can – on the contracting side you can probably do a bit of both. I know they don’t do that much consulting but some of the companies you can do a bit and it’s – in consultancy, you really can’t do any contracting, so I’d definitely rather be contracting rather than consulting.

Interviewer:	OK, would you like to work abroad at all, or travel about or …?

Subject:	Yeah, I would actually. Really like to go and work abroad, but I’m not sure about it.

Interviewer:	What about the company you’re going to work for, do they like have any…?

Subject:	They do have a few jobs abroad, I think. Nothing particularly huge, at the minute, but they do do some stuff.

Interviewer:	Do you think that generally, the career prospects are good in civil engineering?

Subject:	I think so because they need them and they need a lot of civil engineers at the minute. I think, plus being a female it – I do think it gives a bit of an edge. If you’re there and they’ve got 2 equally qualified, equally suitable for the job – 1 male, 1 female, you may tip the balance in your favour, just to cover their quota.

Interviewer:	OK, what about once you’re into the industry? Do you think like the career prospects are good to sort of build and develop your career once you’re…?

Subject:	I think so, yeah, I think – the only problem in the industry is – it’s a bit hard to have babies and still carry on working, but again then you can move, sort of sideways into an office so sort of come off site and go into an office.

Interviewer:	So have you thought about side of things much when you have been deciding what to do?

Subject:	I have actually because you’ve got to think long term career really (yeah) and I did think about that and I thought well there’s plenty of opportunities to sort of move off the site and into an office – sort of design or just doing something sort of semi-consultancy work in the company.

Interviewer:	Do you think that you should have to do that?

Subject:	I don’t think you should have to but er I can’t really see us running round on site, 5 months pregnant – I don’t think it’d be the best of …

Interviewer:	What about, once you’ve actually got children, what do you see as like the conflict between doing site work and having a family?

Subject:	The main problem I can imagine would just be timing, because site hours can be really long, in summer especially. I did meet a couple of people on site – one of the people I worked with, she did have a baby, and she used to have terrible trouble with the nurseries – sort of trying to get people in, like for the long term.

Interviewer:	And do you think that there’s any way round the hours thing? Does that aspect of engineering have to be organised like that? Is there any way that it could be more flexible, do you think?

Subject:	I think probably. I think it depends on the nature of the work they’re doing and the kind of things that you’re doing because certain stuff – and again, a lot of the time, because it’s summer, you’ve obviously still got the daylight, they can have really long hours. In winter, they’re going to be shorter because they don’t have the daylight to do the work and it’s seasonal as well and it depends on, literally, the kind of stuff you’re gonna do.

Interviewer:	OK, are you happy with all the career choices you’ve made, so far?

Subject:	Yeah, I think I am.

Interviewer:	Would you do anything different if you had to do it all again?

Subject:	I’d possibly think about my university choices a bit better, rather than eeny, meeny, miney, mo with the prospectus – ‘cos it was a bit like that (OK) Er, it makes a change to the job interviews, when they ask why did you choose civil engineering – and you’re like, because I love it so much (laughter) rather than random choice.

Interviewer:	Do you think that you’d come up with a different choice then?

Subject:	Er, probably not really, because if I’d sat down and really thought about it, I think I’d probably have still ended up the same way anyway, because like I said it’s the kind of person I am – quite practical, so.

Interviewer:	OK what 5 words would you use to describe engineering characteristics, or culture of engineering?

Subject:	I don’t know – that’s really quite hard, that one. Erm, I know it will be hard work and a bit rewarding, like I said to you where you can actually see – you know physically see the results of what you’ve done and I think that would be very rewarding when you can go back and view it. Come back 10 years down the line you can be like, I did that, I helped do that. Erm, I don’t know any.

Interviewer:	That’s OK. Do you think that the engineering culture is masculine?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Why do you think that it is?

Subject:	I think it’s like I said, because of the image and because people still have an image of it being male and like I said mainly because they speak literally about civil engineering because everybody thinks building site and they think you’re a brickie or something. And I think, especially when –mainly because in civil engineering, nobody knows what it is at all and I think because you say like, mechanical engineering, electrical and everyone says, oh yeah, and they can picture what you do straight away and you say civil and everyone’s like, what’s that then? And you think that – especially, I think, needs to be promoted because no one knows it exists. I think that’s part of the problem with it being masculine is people – because they don’t know what it is and you say, oh it’s like building things and then they think building site and loads of men running around and things.

Interviewer:	So do you think that’s like a false perception really?

Subject:	Partly and just a general lack of information, I think.

Interviewer:	Ok do you think that will stay like that or do you think that situation will get better?

Subject:	I think it will get better because gradually people realise more as more and more women go into engineering, it’s not quite as surprising an idea for people now, that you get girls doing engineering stuff. It’s fairly – to come here it’s accepted that you’re going to have girls doing engineering. I think partly because of its nature – it’s very practical and hands on, I think it will probably stay more male orientated just because of the way it is.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that any aspects of the engineering culture could cause any problems or be problematic for you?

Subject:	I don’t think so – I’ve not experienced any major – major issues with it, really. I think as long as you don’t meet anyone with very, very big issues about females in the industry, it will be fine. I think as a general rule they’re just like, yeah, girls – whatever. That’s a general attitude I’ve found – it’s just like yeah, you’re a girl doing engineering, OK.

Interviewer:	Do you think that you have to work harder to prove yourself because you’re a woman or…?

Subject:	I don’t think so. If you can do your job, then you can do it and they’ll say fine, you can do it.

Interviewer:	OK, that’s good. Do you think that your educational experiences differ from other students like in Social Sciences or business or something like that?

Subject:	I think so because we do stupid or apparently stupid things like when we were wandering around surveying. You know, we were wandering around the football pitch, carrying all the surveying equipment and they’re like, what are you doing? Whereas they spend all their time in their lectures and stuff, and that’s a very non-practical way. We actually do more practical stuff. And in that respect I think, because you see some girls who want to get really dressed up to go to lectures and you can’t imagine them banging pegs into a football field for half an hour.

Interviewer:	OK, well that’s all the questions that I have for you, unless there’s anything else you’d like to add at all? (no) OK thank you very much.

Then we will compare it to their experiences when they’re actually in the industry and what we’re really trying to do is improve the retention of women in the industry. So we’re looking to see if work meets women’s expectations and things like that. My mum was like try engineering, you haven’t read it. I thought, oh that sounds fun, it’s quite me. Sort of you know, practical work basically – so I’m not sitting around, in an office. I get bored and that’s where I came from, really no major reason.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you didn’t really have any careers advice that pointed you in that direction?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I didn’t have a single careers interview through school no, they don’t really mention – like I say they seem to be very, well old school as it were. Oxford, Cambridge – trying to send as many people as they could off to do law and history and English and things.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, you said that your mum helped you decide on engineering – has your family been quite supportive then of the fact that you…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I mean basically it was I thought about it, thought it was a good idea. I mean my parents weren’t particularly fussed.
